title: How Megalodon Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the megalodon, an extinct giant shark that lived roughly 20 million to 1.5 million years ago. They cover how its teeth and centrum were discovered and mistaken for dragon tongues, how fossilization preserves teeth and vertebral centra, growth rings used to estimate age, its size and bite force, a fossil nursery found off Panama and South Carolina, its worldwide distribution, its prey (whales), and a 2016 study attributing its extinction to prey diversity loss rather than climate change. They discuss its relation to mako and porbeagle sharks, cryptozoology and the megamouth and coelacanth finds, Discovery Channel's fake megalodon documentary and the backlash, and megalodon tooth sales. The episode ends with a listener mail about the US Family and Medical Leave Act and paid parental leave.

segments.title: Opening banter and megalodon introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about bus trips and introduce the megalodon as a real giant shark, roughly school-bus sized.

segments.title: Megalodon teeth and early misidentification
segments.summary: Megalodon teeth were compared with great white and T. rex teeth. Early finders thought the fossils were dragon tongues until Nicholas Steno identified them as teeth in 1667.

segments.title: Fossilization of shark cartilage and centra
segments.summary: Shark skeletons are mostly cartilage, which decays, but teeth and the centrum fossilize by mineral replacement, which is why megalodon remains survive.

segments.title: Timeline and growth rings
segments.summary: Megalodon lived about 20 to 1.5 million years ago, with no overlap with dinosaurs or humans. Growth rings in the centra indicate age and growth rates.

segments.title: Global distribution, nursery site, and size
segments.summary: Megalodon teeth have been found on every continent except Antarctica. A 2009 fossil find of baby megalodons in a nursery, reported near Panama and South Carolina, suggested pups about 20 feet long. Megalodons weighed 50 to 100 tons and reportedly ate large amounts of food daily.

segments.title: Bite force, jaws, and diet
segments.summary: The hosts describe the megalodon's bite as strong enough to crush a whale skull, and note reconstructed jaws are resin with a roughly seven-foot mouth diameter. Teeth marks on whale bones show whales were prey.

segments.title: Extinction, relation to mako sharks, and cryptozoology
segments.summary: A study from the Zurich Paleontological Institute found that the megalodon's extinction seems tied to less diverse prey and competition from smaller predators such as orcas, not climate change. Megalodon is now thought to be related to mako and porbeagle sharks, not great whites. The hosts discuss living-fossil finds like the coelacanth and megamouth shark, and why megalodon is unlikely to survive today.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Brief sign-off, pointing listeners to the website.
